messages.subject: Re: simulating pond temperatures
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tiem,
No new approaches I'm afraid besides those two.
All the best,
Mike

On Friday, September 1, 2023 at 1:03:20 AM UTC+10 Tiem van der Deure wrote:
> Dear Mike,
>
> I was wondering if this is still the best way to generate temperature profiles for water bodies, or if there is a way to run the container model without this workaround?
>
> I am working on temperature responses of freshwater snails and this could be a great fit.
>
> Best, Tiem
>
>
>
> On Thursday, 18 March 2021 at 10:38:16 UTC+1 Michael Kearney wrote:
> > Dear Dennis,
> >
> > You can use the ectotherm mode or the microclimate model to simulate pond depths and temperatures, but in a bit of a kludgy way.
> >
> > For the microclimate model approach, you simulate a clay-based substrate and put a multiplier on the rainfall to simulate a catchment. I've found this can predict pond depths extremely well for a shallow wetland - it captures both the rain input and the evaporation/seepage output mechanistically, but not the water temperature. To get a rough prediction of water temperature you can use the water-logged soil temperatures for different depths to get a rough estimate.
> >
> > Alternatively you can use the 'container' model of the ectotherm model, which simulates an open-topped container either sitting on the surface (like a paddling pool) or sunk into the ground, and you can optionally put a hole in it (constant drainage per day) and vary the fraction of the surface that evaporates (to simulate it being partly covered). This can be computationally more intensive but will give a more accurate estimate of what the water temperature would be at the centre of the pond.
> >
> > The main thing of course is to have some good data with which to test it. Down the track we may finish integrating the 'General Lake Model' with NicheMapR, which is a proper fully-physical model of a water body with stratification etc.
> >
> > I’ve put some example code together (using the micro_usa function) below to show you how to implement the two approaches. Note the ectotherm model simulation took about 25 mins for the 2 year simulation! And also note that you'll have to install the latest version of the ectotherm model for the code below to work because there was a bug in the error trapping preventing 'conthole' from being different to zero or one, but it's fixed as of today.
> >
> > All the best,
> > Mike
> >
> > library(NicheMapR)
> >
> > # microclimate model approach
> >
> > # define textural soil properties for clay
> > soilpro <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 6, ncol = 5)
> > colnames(soilpro) <- c('depth', 'blkdens', 'clay', 'silt', 'sand')
> > soilpro[,1] <- c(2.5, 7.5, 22.5, 45, 80, 150)
> > soilpro[,2] <- 1.4 # bulk density (Mg/m3)
> > soilpro[,3] <- 90 # % clay
> > soilpro[,4] <- 0.0 # % silt
> > soilpro[,5] <- 10 # % sand
> > DEP <- c(0, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 90, 200) # Soil nodes (cm)
> >
> > # get hydraulic properties for given soil
> > soil.hydro <- pedotransfer(soilpro = as.data.frame(soilpro), DEP = DEP)
> > PE <- soil.hydro$PE
> > BB <- soil.hydro$BB
> > BD <- soil.hydro$BD
> > KS <- soil.hydro$KS
> > BulkDensity <- BD[seq(1, 19, 2)]
> >
> > rainmult <- 4.5 # Rainfall multiplier to reflect catchment (1 will result in unadjusted rainfall)
> > maxpool <- 500 # maximium pooling depth (mm), i.e. wetland depth
> > LAI <- 0 # leaf area index (zero so no transpiration)
> > cap <- 0 # do not simulate the organic cap layer
> > soilgrids <- 0 # don't use SoilGrids soil database for thermal properties
> >
> > micro <- micro_usa(PE = PE, BB = BB, BD = BD, KS = KS, rainmult = rainmult, maxpool = maxpool, LAI = LAI, cap = cap, soilgrids = soilgrids)
> > metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
> > soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil)
> > wetlandDepths<-as.data.frame(cbind(dates,as.data.frame(metout$POOLDEP)))
> > colnames(wetlandDepths) <- c('dates', 'pond depth')
> >
> > # get closest soil depths for each wetland depth
> > depth <- apply(as.matrix(wetlandDepths$depth / 10), 1, function(x) which.min(abs(x - DEP)))
> > depth <- depth - 2 # actually choose 2 nodes shallower to better approximate amplitude
> > depth[depth <= 0] <- 1 # step above produces some values below one - correct this
> >
> > # now get the soil temperatures for the corresponding wetland depths
> > wetlandTemps <- as.data.frame(as.numeric(soil[cbind(seq_along(depth + 3), depth + 3)]))
> > wetlandTemps <- cbind(dates, wetlandTemps) # append dates
> > colnames(wetlandTemps) <- c('dates', 'pond temperature')
> >
> > par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
> > plot(wetlandDepths, type = 'l', ylim = c(0, 500), main = 'microclimate model prediction')
> > plot(wetlandTemps, type = 'l', ylim = c(-20, 50))
> >
> > # ectotherm model approach
> >
> > # container model parameters
> > container <- 1 # Run the water body/container model? (aquatic start of life cycle, e.g. frog or mosquito)
> > conth <- 500 # Cylindrical container/pond height (mm)
> > contw <- 10000 # Cylindrical container/pond diameter (mm)
> > contype <- 1 # Is 'container' sitting on the surface, like a bucket (0) or sunk into the ground like a pond (1)
> > rainmult <- 4.5 # Rainfall multiplier to reflect catchment (1 will result in unadjusted rainfall)
> > continit <- 0 # Initial container water level (cm)
> > conthole <- 10 # Daily (or hourly if rainhr vector filled) loss of height (mm) due to 'hole' in container (e.g. infiltration to soil, drawdown from water tank)
> > contonly <- 1 # Just run the container model and quit?
> > contwet <- 100 # % of container surface acting as a free water exchanger
> >
> > # run the ectotherm model (this is quite slow! ~ 25 mins)
> > ecto <- ectotherm(container = container, conth = conth, contw = contw, contype = contype,
> >                   rainmult = rainmult, continit = continit, conthole = conthole,
> >                   contonly = contonly, contwet = contwet)
> > environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
> > plot(micro$dates, environ$CONDEP, type = 'l', ylab = 'container depth', xlab = 'date', ylim = c(0, 500), main = 'ectotherm model prediction')
> > plot(micro$dates, environ$TC, type = 'l', ylab = 'water temperature', xlab = 'date', ylim = c(-20, 50))
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, March 18, 2021 at 6:44:51 PM UTC+11 dennis....@googlemail.com wrote:
> > > Dear Mike,
> > >
> > > in your Ecography paper introducing the NicheMapR R package you announce another study introducing the ectotherm model to simulate pond conditons
> > >
> > > "The ectotherm model also has scope to estimate transient heat budgets, and thus stored heat, QS, but without thermoregulatory behaviour. This functionality can also be used to estimate water temperatures in a ‘bucket model’ simulation of a container filling with rainwater which can be used to simulate ponds and other waterbodies under certain assumptions. These aspects of the model will be described elsewhere."
> > >
> > > Having temperature profiles for pond strata would be awsome and very helpful for my projects. Is there already a descrption how to simulate this kind of pond microclimates?
> > >
> > > Thank you so much in advance,
> > > best wishes
> > > Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Professor Kearney，

I am currently using the endoR function to simulate mammoth physiological responses in historical contexts. I have a couple of questions and would greatly appreciate your guidance.

1. QGEN Variable: During the simulation, I've noticed that the "QGEN" variable sometimes takes negative values, but the "SUCCESS" variable consistently shows 1 (indicating success). Could you please explain the significance of the "QGEN" variable and how it impacts the simulation results?

2. Food Requirements: There are two parameters, "O2_L" representing oxygen consumption rate (L/h) and "QGEN." I would like to inquire about which parameter, 'O2_L' or 'QGEN,' is more suitable for calculating mammoth food requirements. Your insights on this matter would be invaluable.

3. NicheMapR: I'm aware that Niche Mapper.exe can directly calculate food requirements. Is there a way to convert the results obtained from NicheMapR into food requirements, and if so, could you provide some guidance on this process?

Your expertise and assistance would greatly contribute to my research. Thank you for considering my questions.

Warm regards,

Yize Liu

messages.subject: Re: Queries regarding simulation model parameters and nicheMapR data conversion
messages.subject_clean: Queries regarding simulation model parameters and nicheMapR data conversion
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yize Liu,

1. QGEN is the prediction from the model of metabolic heat production - it is the key thing that the model predicts. QGEN (reported in Watts) must not go below your stated 'QBASAL' (though this isn't a great name for this output - it may not be basal, it's whatever your lower possible limit on metabolic rate is). If it's lower than your QBASAL, then the model couldn't find a way to keep predicted metabolic rate at that value, and the inference is death. 'SUCCESS' just means that a solution was found for the heat balance, even though it's not a biologically plausible one (or even a physically plausible one - if the result is negative!).

2. The O2_L is a rough conversion from metabolic rate in Watts to what the oxygen consumption rate should be. The latter is often used as an indirect measure of metabolic rate. QGEN is the direct metabolic rate quantifier - energy used per time.

3. Conversion of predicted energy requirements from the output of the model is something worth working out yourself so you understand the biology of it. The predicted metabolic rate from the model tells you part of their obligatory energy requirements. So, if you know the food energy content and the digestive efficiency you can go from metabolic rate to required food. It's a basic physiological calculation and there are lots of examples out there.

Hope that helps.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Questions regarding incorporating surface water (wetlands) as input for gridded microclimate modeling
messages.subject_clean: Questions regarding incorporating surface water (wetlands) as input for gridded microclimate modeling
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Kearney,

I am an MS student working on a research project where a key step is to produce gridded hourly rasters of microclimate air temperatures at the surface of wetlands and adjacent upland areas. I plan to use the ERA5 hourly reanalysis and various terrain/vegetation data as inputs. The NicheMapR-microclima workflow seems appropriate to produce gridded outputs at the resolution I need.  I’ve reviewed the posts and relevant papers where the clay rainfall catchment method to simulate pond temperatures was used, but these seem to be mostly for partially-to fully-submerged ectotherms. My aim is use this for a semi-aquatic endotherm that spends most of its time feeding or loafing on the surface of the water (dabbling duck). I am inquiring if this method also is applicable for simulating air temperature at the surface of bodies of water? If so, can it be readily integrated into the NicheMapR-microclima gridded output workflow?

Thank you for your time and consideration. Please let me know if you have any additional questions regarding the information and inquiry provided.

Respectfully,

Joseph McGovern

messages.subject: Re: Questions regarding incorporating surface water (wetlands) as input for gridded microclimate modeling
messages.subject_clean: Questions regarding incorporating surface water (wetlands) as input for gridded microclimate modeling
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joseph,

The microclimate model approach of simulating a clay pan can give you a good estimate of wetland depth, and the 'bucket model' approach in the ectotherm model will predict the 'core temperature' of the bucket, but neither are really meant for predicting microclimates at the surface of a water body. It really is a job for a hydrological model like the general lake model <https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/12/473/2019/gmd-12-473-2019.html>. The endotherm model can be used to simulate a duck's energetics when sitting on the surface or diving. There are some good papers on this by Warren Porter and colleagues on seabirds <https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/212/15/2483/18443/Thermodynamic-modelling-predicts-energetic>. It is specific about the dorsal and ventral environment and you can also change the 'fluid' to water.

Note that whatever you do the predictions will be computationally expensive and you might get just as much of an understanding by some judicious point analyses rather than generating (admittedly less satisfying) gridded outputs. At least it is worth exploring and carefully testing how well you can make predictions using points first.

Hope that helps.

All the best,
Mike

Hi Joseph,
It really isn't set up for this - you could see what you get if you treat the substrate as 100% wet and set the soil properties to water but in reality you get vertical and lateral mixing and that is the sort of thing that the lake models do.
All the best,
Mike

On Thursday, September 28, 2023 at 7:37:36 AM UTC+10 josephm...@gmail.com wrote:
> Mike,
>
> Thank you very much for your response; this is very helpful information. Just to clarify further, is it not advisable to try to use any microclimate model to predict air temperatures just above (e.g., 5 cm) the surface of a body of water? We are primarily concerned with estimating fine-scale air temperatures and would like to know if we can incorporate characteristics of the radiative/reflective environment that characterizes a body of water in the microclimate modeling setting to do this. Otherwise we will definitely look into the general lake model for our purposes.
>
> Thank you so much for your help and advice.
>
> Best regards,
>
> Joseph
>
> On Tue, Sep 19, 2023 at 2:28 AM NicheMapR <nich...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Hi Joseph,
> >
> > The microclimate model approach of simulating a clay pan can give you a good estimate of wetland depth, and the 'bucket model' approach in the ectotherm model will predict the 'core temperature' of the bucket, but neither are really meant for predicting microclimates at the surface of a water body. It really is a job for a hydrological model like the general lake model <https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/12/473/2019/gmd-12-473-2019.html>. The endotherm model can be used to simulate a duck's energetics when sitting on the surface or diving. There are some good papers on this by Warren Porter and colleagues on seabirds <https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/212/15/2483/18443/Thermodynamic-modelling-predicts-energetic>. It is specific about the dorsal and ventral environment and you can also change the 'fluid' to water.
> >
> > Note that whatever you do the predictions will be computationally expensive and you might get just as much of an understanding by some judicious point analyses rather than generating (admittedly less satisfying) gridded outputs. At least it is worth exploring and carefully testing how well you can make predictions using points first.
> >
> > Hope that helps.
> >
> > All the best,
> > Mike
> >
> > On Tuesday, September 19, 2023 at 7:26:57 AM UTC+10 josephm...@gmail.com wrote:
> > >
> > > Dear Dr. Kearney,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I am an MS student working on a research project where a key step is to produce gridded hourly rasters of microclimate air temperatures at the surface of wetlands and adjacent upland areas. I plan to use the ERA5 hourly reanalysis and various terrain/vegetation data as inputs. The NicheMapR-microclima workflow seems appropriate to produce gridded outputs at the resolution I need.  I’ve reviewed the posts and relevant papers where the clay rainfall catchment method to simulate pond temperatures was used, but these seem to be mostly for partially-to fully-submerged ectotherms. My aim is use this for a semi-aquatic endotherm that spends most of its time feeding or loafing on the surface of the water (dabbling duck). I am inquiring if this method also is applicable for simulating air temperature at the surface of bodies of water? If so, can it be readily integrated into the NicheMapR-microclima gridded output workflow?
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Thank you for your time and consideration. Please let me know if you have any additional questions regarding the information and inquiry provided.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Respectfully,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Joseph McGovern
